extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP litigators, in-house counsel and other practitioners interested in Federal Circuit anticipation law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and case-law principles for evaluating patent invalidity by anticipation (including inherent anticipation, claim preamble effect, prior-art qualification under §102, testimonial evidence, and design-patent anticipation). Summarizes Federal Circuit holdings and tests relevant to anticipation determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent anticipation standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation by inherent disclosure is appropriate only when the reference discloses prior art that must necessarily include the unstated limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Transclean: inherent anticipation requires that the unstated limitation be necessarily present in the prior art reference. Example: King Pharms. — ordinary results of taking metaxalone with food (increased bioavailability) were inherent in prior art dosing, so claims were inherently anticipated. Courts will hold newly discovered benefits of old processes to be inherent in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble is non-limiting unless relied upon in prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Preamble language that merely states the purpose or intended use of an invention is generally not treated as limiting the scope of the claim; a preamble becomes limiting only when the patentee clearly relies on it during prosecution to distinguish the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marrin v. Griffin: district court and Federal Circuit found a 'for permitting' preamble to be a statement of intended use and not a limitation because patentees did not rely on it during prosecution; amendment history showed patentees expressly conceded the 'writing means' was not a limitation. Dissent (Judge Newman) warns against deleting limitations stated in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informing/mental-step limitations do not cure lack of novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding an 'informing' limitation (or similar non-transformative step) to an anticipated claim does not cure lack of novelty; informational steps that do not transform the substantive process are not sufficient to create novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King Pharms.: court held that informing a patient about a drug's benefit does not transform the process of taking the drug with food and therefore does not avoid inherent anticipation. District court's Bilski analysis aside, novelty cannot be saved by merely adding informational or advisory steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-reference rule: single reference must disclose every claim limitation (expressly or inherently)
rubrics_metrics.description: To anticipate, a single prior art reference must disclose each and every limitation of the claimed invention, either explicitly or inherently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited repeatedly (Finisar, Orion): anticipation requires one reference that contains all claim limitations. Incorporation by reference of other material is possible, but courts treat what is properly incorporated as part of the single reference (see incorporation-by-reference rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation is a question of fact and requires clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claim is anticipated is a question of fact for the finder; invalidity by anticipation must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, and appellate review of a jury trial on anticipation is for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orion v. Hyundai: Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict where it found Hyundai showed by clear and convincing evidence that the printed brochure (with testimonial support) anticipated the claim. Cases cite Yoon Ja Kim for the clear-and-convincing standard and note substantial-evidence review on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimonial and documentary evidence can support that a printed reference anticipates
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony from experts and third-party fact witnesses, and documentary evidence, can establish that a printed publication or brochure anticipates a claim by showing the reference (as used) disclosed required limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orion and Verizon examples: expert/fact witnesses explained how an advertised system generated proposals; Cox's expert (author of the reference) provided detailed testimony that enabled a jury to find anticipation. The newsletter emphasizes the benefits of supporting anticipatory references with testimonial and fact evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration requirement for inventor testimony depends on context
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a corroboration requirement when inventor testimony is offered to assert a prior invention (offensive use under §102(g)); but inventor testimony offered defensively to rebut an anticipation attack may not require the same corroboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: i4i: where documentary evidence of prior art was imperfect, inventor testimony offered by the patentee to respond to the defendant's anticipation attack was held not to require corroboration in that defensive context. Cases cited: Finnigan, TypeRight, Texas Digital for the corroboration rule when used offensively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation-by-reference determination is a question of law for the court
rubrics_metrics.description: If incorporation by reference is relevant to an anticipation determination, it is the court's role (a question of law) to decide what material beyond the host document constitutes the single reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verizon v. Cox: Federal Circuit held that the court must determine what, if anything, has been properly incorporated by reference; failure to instruct the jury on this was harmless where expert testimony allowed a finding of anticipation without incorporated material.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. §102(e) priority date can reach back to provisional applications (subject to §112 support)
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. patent may qualify as prior art under §102(e) based on its earliest effective filing date; a provisional application can be treated as 'an application' under §102(e) such that the patent's effective date may reach back to the provisional, provided the earlier-filed specification provides written-description support under Section 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Giacomini: Federal Circuit affirmed that a provisional application is an 'application' for §102(e) purposes if it discloses the claimed invention (i.e., provides written description support). Practical effect: watch provisional content if relying on or defending against §102(e) rejections/anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent anticipation: ordinary observer test is sole test; point-of-novelty abolished
rubrics_metrics.description: For design patents, the Federal Circuit confirmed that the ordinary observer test — not the point-of-novelty test — is the sole test for determining anticipation (and infringement). The inquiry asks whether an ordinary observer would believe the designs are substantially the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Int'l Seaway Trading v. Walgreens (following Egyptian Goddess): abolishes point-of-novelty test to keep anticipation and infringement tests identical. The review must consider the state of the prior art: when the claimed design is close to the prior art, small differences will be important to the ordinary observer. Cites Peters maxim: 'That which infringes, if later, would anticipate, if earlier.'
